essays.title: Grammar Before Creativity: A False Sequence
essays.prompt: In order to become good writers, students must first learn the formal rules of grammar and structure; only after mastering these rules should they be given the freedom to write creatively.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: The claim that formal rules must precede creative freedom rests on an appealing but misleading metaphor: that writing is built the way a house is built, foundation first, ornamentation later. In practice, the development of a writer rarely follows so tidy a sequence, and treating rule-mastery as a gatekeeping requirement for creative expression risks producing technically correct but lifeless prose. While structural competence is undeniably valuable, I disagree that it must be acquired before creative freedom is granted; the two are better cultivated together, each sharpening the other.

Consider how children actually learn language. A five-year-old telling an elaborate, ungrammatical story about a dragon is already engaged in the central work of writing: organizing experience into narrative, choosing vivid images, building suspense. If a teacher intervened at that moment to withhold storytelling until every verb agreed with its subject, the child would likely lose the very motivation that makes grammar worth learning in the first place. Motivation matters enormously in skill acquisition, and creative expression is often what supplies it. Students revise their grammar most willingly when they are revising a sentence they already care about, not a decontextualized worksheet exercise.

There is also a subtler cost to the sequential model: it implies that grammar is a fixed set of rules to be mastered once, whereas skilled writers continually renegotiate the rules for effect. A fragment used for emphasis, a deliberately run-on sentence to convey breathlessness, an unconventional structure that mirrors a character's confusion — these are not lapses but choices, and students who only ever encounter "correct" grammar in isolation from creative purpose struggle to recognize when departing from convention is itself the more sophisticated move. Writers such as Toni Morrison and Cormac McCarthy became masters of unconventional punctuation not despite understanding grammar but because they understood it well enough to bend it purposefully; that understanding, however, developed through sustained creative practice, not as a prerequisite to it.

None of this means formal instruction is unnecessary. A student who has never learned to identify a sentence fragment will struggle to control one deliberately, and there is real value in explicit grammar lessons that give students a shared vocabulary for revising their own drafts. The strongest classrooms I have observed do not sequence these skills but interleave them: a brief lesson on comma splices is immediately applied to revising a personal essay the student has already drafted, so the rule serves the writing rather than preceding it as an abstract hurdle.

In the end, the sequential model gets the relationship backward. Grammar is not the foundation on which creativity is later built; it is one of several tools, alongside imagination and voice, that developing writers pick up simultaneously and apply with increasing precision. A curriculum that delays creative expression until formal correctness is achieved risks producing students who can diagram a sentence but have nothing they want to say with it — a far greater failure than an occasional misplaced modifier.

essays.title: The Limits of a Universal Requirement
essays.prompt: To best prepare students for success after graduation, universities should require every student, regardless of major, to complete coursework in computer programming.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the recommendation and explain how these consequences shape your position.
paragraphs: Universities exist to prepare students for a world that is, by definition, not yet fully known to the people designing the curriculum. Given how central computing has become to modern work, the recommendation that every student study programming is understandable. But a universal requirement is the wrong instrument for a legitimate goal: it would consume scarce curricular space that many students would use more productively elsewhere, and it mistakes exposure to a skill for genuine competence in it.

The strongest argument for the recommendation is that programming teaches a transferable habit of mind — breaking a problem into precise, testable steps — that benefits students far outside computer science. This is true, and it is the recommendation's best justification. A single required course, however, is unlikely to instill that habit durably. Learning to think computationally takes sustained practice, not a single introductory semester wedged between other requirements; more likely, an unmotivated student satisfies the requirement, passes a syntax-focused exam, and retains almost nothing a year later. If transferable reasoning is truly the goal, other disciplines — formal logic, statistics, even a well-taught philosophy proof course — cultivate the same habit and may do so more effectively for students who have no interest in code itself.

There is also an opportunity cost the recommendation understates. Universities already require students to balance a major, a set of general-education courses, and often a foreign language or lab science within four years. Adding a mandatory programming course does not appear from nowhere; it displaces something else a student would have taken — an elective in their intended field, a study-abroad term, a course that might have been the deciding factor in a job offer. For a philosophy major heading toward law school or a nursing student whose curriculum is already saturated with required clinical hours, a semester of programming is a poor trade against courses more directly relevant to their goals.

None of this means programming instruction is not worth offering broadly. Universities should make introductory computing courses widely available, well-taught, and explicitly framed around real applications in students' own fields — a data-analysis module for economics majors, a bioinformatics primer for biology students — so that motivated students across disciplines can opt in without artificial barriers. What should be resisted is treating "requirement" as a synonym for "value." A university's obligation is to prepare each student for a specific and varied set of futures, not to hedge against uncertainty by mandating the same narrow skill set for everyone.

If the goal is graduates who can reason precisely and adapt to a technology-saturated workplace, the answer lies in making such reasoning central across the curriculum rather than isolating it in a single required course that most students will complete without ever internalizing its underlying value.

essays.title: Two Obligations, Not One
essays.prompt: Universities should evaluate professors primarily on their skill as teachers rather than on their record of scholarly research, since teaching, not research, is a university's core obligation to its students.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which it is based. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the claim and the reason might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: The reasoning behind this claim assumes that a university has a single core obligation to a single audience — its students — and that everything else, including research, is at best a secondary activity competing for a professor's time. This premise is where the claim goes wrong. A university's obligation is not only to the students currently enrolled but to the advancement and transmission of knowledge itself, and research is not a distraction from that mission but a constitutive part of it. I therefore disagree with both the claim and the reason it rests on, though I agree that teaching quality is currently undervalued in many tenure and promotion processes.

Consider what students actually gain from being taught by active researchers. A professor who is still investigating open questions in her field teaches differently than one who is only transmitting settled textbook knowledge: she can describe not just what is known but how it came to be known, where the field's genuine uncertainties lie, and what a live research problem actually looks like from the inside. Students preparing for graduate study or research careers benefit enormously from this exposure, and even students who will never conduct research themselves gain a more honest picture of how knowledge is produced — a form of intellectual literacy no purely pedagogical training can substitute for.

There is also a practical problem with the claim's implicit solution. If evaluation shifted to rest primarily on teaching skill, universities would face a serious recruitment problem: the most capable emerging scholars, whose research reputations open doors to funding, collaboration, and visibility for their institutions, would migrate toward universities that continued to reward research, leaving teaching-primary institutions with a talent pool skewed toward those who could not otherwise succeed in the field. A policy meant to elevate teaching could inadvertently depress the quality of who is available to do it.

Where the claim has real force is in exposing a genuine imbalance: many institutions currently treat teaching evaluations as a formality while research output drives tenure decisions with near-total weight, and professors who are gifted teachers but modest researchers are too often pushed out or denied advancement. This is a legitimate problem, but the solution is not to invert the imbalance — replacing one lopsided standard with another — but to weight both criteria seriously and evaluate teaching with the same rigor currently reserved for research, through peer observation, structured student feedback over time, and evidence of course redesign, rather than end-of-semester satisfaction surveys alone.

A university that asked only "can this person teach well?" would be a better trade school but a worse university. Its core obligation is broader than direct instruction; it includes producing the knowledge that instruction eventually transmits, and any evaluation system that neglects this dual mission serves neither students nor scholarship well.

essays.title: Structure as a Condition for Freedom, Not Its Opposite
essays.prompt: Some educators believe that students learn best when allowed to pursue their own interests with minimal structure. Others believe that students learn best within a clearly defined curriculum with consistent external benchmarks. Which view more closely aligns with your own position?
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
paragraphs: These two views are usually presented as opposites, but the sharpest version of each actually depends on a claim about the other. The interest-driven view assumes that structure suppresses the curiosity it should be cultivating; the benchmark-driven view assumes that unstructured exploration produces gaps a student cannot later fill. My own position sits closer to the second view, but only because I think it is possible to build structure that creates room for genuine interest rather than crowding it out — a synthesis the either/or framing of the prompt tends to obscure.

The case for minimal structure rests on a real observation: students retain far more when they are intrinsically motivated, and assigned curricula frequently fail to connect with what a given student already finds compelling. A student obsessed with basketball statistics who is never allowed to bring that interest into a math class is being taught a subject stripped of the one hook likely to make it stick. This is a genuine cost of rigid, uniform curricula, and educators who dismiss it are not taking learning science seriously.

Yet the case for a defined curriculum with consistent benchmarks addresses a problem the interest-driven view does not solve: cumulative subjects, like mathematics or a foreign language, require a sequence of skills where later concepts genuinely depend on earlier ones. A ten-year-old who spends a semester following only her own curiosity may produce fascinating independent projects while never learning long division — not because she lacks ability, but because nothing forced the sequence to occur, and children are rarely positioned to know in advance which foundational skills they will need years later. External benchmarks exist precisely to catch this kind of gap before it becomes difficult to close.

What tips my position toward structure is that the strongest version of curriculum-driven teaching is not opposed to student interest; it uses required benchmarks as a floor, not a ceiling. A well-designed cumulative curriculum in mathematics still leaves room for a student to explore basketball statistics as the vehicle through which she learns about averages, variance, and probability — the benchmark specifies what must be learned, not that interest must be excluded from how it is taught. The unstructured model, by contrast, has no comparable safeguard against foundational gaps; a student's curiosity, however genuine, cannot substitute for a sequence she does not yet know she needs.

I therefore side with structured, benchmark-driven education, but I would resist any version of it that treats structure and interest as substitutes rather than complements. The best classrooms I have seen are not the least structured ones, nor the most rigid ones, but those where a fixed set of required outcomes is taught through content flexible enough to meet a student's existing curiosity partway.

essays.title: Narrative Evaluation: Right Diagnosis, Incomplete Cure
essays.prompt: Some universities have adopted a policy of eliminating all letter grades in undergraduate courses, replacing them with narrative evaluations of student performance. What are your views on this policy?
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the policy and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: Letter grades compress a semester of uneven, multidimensional work into a single symbol, and it is easy to see why some universities have concluded that this compression does real damage — flattening the distinction between a student who mastered the material after a rocky start and one who coasted on prior knowledge, and encouraging students to optimize for the grade rather than for genuine understanding. The policy of replacing letter grades with narrative evaluation responds to a real problem. But I view it as a well-intentioned solution that, implemented on its own, creates new problems at least as serious as the ones it solves.

The strongest case for narrative evaluation is pedagogical: a paragraph explaining what a student understood well, where their reasoning broke down, and what would most improve their next attempt is simply more useful feedback than a B+. Students report, and research on formative assessment supports, that specific qualitative feedback changes behavior more effectively than a numerical or letter summary, which students often read only to check their standing before discarding the substance. If the goal is learning rather than sorting, narrative evaluation is the more honest instrument.

The trouble is that universities do not operate in isolation from the systems that consume their evaluations. Graduate admissions committees, employers, and scholarship boards routinely compare applicants across institutions using GPA as a rough, imperfect, but fast filtering tool. A university that abolishes letter grades does not abolish the need for comparison; it merely shifts the burden of comparison onto outside readers who must now interpret dozens of narrative paragraphs per applicant, with no shared rubric, no institutional calibration, and far less time than a professor spent writing them. Students from the reformed university may find themselves at a real disadvantage against otherwise identical applicants whose transcripts translate instantly into a number.

There is also an internal cost: narrative evaluations, however well-intentioned, are exceptionally labor-intensive to write well and consistent. A professor teaching four sections of 40 students each cannot produce 160 individualized, substantive narratives every semester without either delegating the task in ways that undermine its personal value or defaulting, under time pressure, to a handful of templated phrases that function as grades in disguise — "excellent effort," "solid grasp of core concepts" — without the disguise's honesty.

My own view is that the diagnosis behind this policy is correct and the remedy is half right: narrative feedback genuinely improves learning and should be expanded, but it should supplement rather than fully replace a summary metric, so that the internal benefits of rich feedback do not come at the cost of external legibility that students still need when they leave the university's walls.

essays.title: Subjectivity Is Not a Special Problem for Art
essays.prompt: Government funding for the arts should be eliminated; because artistic value is inherently subjective, public money should not be spent on projects that only some citizens will appreciate.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the claim might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: The argument against public arts funding rests on a premise that sounds rigorous but proves too much: that government should not spend money on anything whose value is subjectively assessed and unevenly appreciated by the public. If that premise were consistently applied, it would eliminate far more than arts funding — public funding for parks, historic preservation, even certain scientific research whose payoff is uncertain and unevenly distributed would fall under the same objection. I disagree with the claim, because subjectivity of value is a poor test for what government may legitimately fund.

Governments routinely fund goods precisely because private markets underfund them, and this is as true of art as of basic research. A publicly funded theater or museum program frequently provides access to citizens who could not otherwise afford it, generating a form of value — cultural literacy, civic identity, historical memory — that is diffuse, hard to price, and therefore chronically underfunded by private donors and ticket sales alone. The subjectivity of an individual's aesthetic judgment does not mean the broader social function of art is illusory; a national theater does not need every citizen to enjoy every production for its existence to serve a genuine public interest, any more than a public library needs every book to be read by every patron.

There is also a practical inconsistency in singling out art. Public funding routinely supports goods that only some citizens directly use or value: agricultural subsidies benefit farmers and rural communities far more than urban ones; funding for a particular scientific discipline benefits some fields of inquiry more than others that compete for the same limited grants. If uneven appreciation were disqualifying, most categories of public spending would need to be eliminated, not merely the arts. The claim's reasoning, taken seriously, is far more radical than its narrow application to art suggests, which is itself a sign that the reasoning is not being applied consistently.

I do think the claim points toward a real and worthwhile concern: public arts funding should be accountable, transparent about how projects are selected, and responsive to the range of tastes and communities it serves, rather than concentrated in a narrow set of institutions that primarily serve already-privileged audiences. That is a legitimate critique of how arts funding is administered, and it is worth taking seriously. But it is a critique of implementation, not a case for elimination.

Eliminating arts funding because value is subjective would not make government spending more objective; it would simply relocate the same problem to other categories of spending while abandoning a domain — public access to cultural and creative life — that markets alone have never reliably provided for everyone.

essays.title: Efficiency Is a Poor Proxy for Democratic Health
essays.prompt: The health of a democracy is better measured by how peacefully it handles internal disagreement than by how efficiently its government makes decisions.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: Efficiency is a seductive metric because it is easy to observe: a government that passes legislation quickly, implements policy without prolonged debate, and avoids gridlock looks, on the surface, healthier than one mired in dispute. But this appearance is misleading, and I largely agree with the statement, because efficiency measures how fast a system moves, not whether it is moving toward outcomes that reflect its citizens' genuine, often conflicting interests — and a government that suppresses disagreement to achieve speed is efficient at the wrong thing.

The clearest illustration is what efficient but non-peaceful systems tend to sacrifice. Authoritarian governments are frequently more "efficient" by narrow procedural measures: decisions are made faster because there is no meaningful opposition to negotiate with. Yet this efficiency comes at the cost of exactly the disagreement- processing function that healthy democracies exist to perform — surfacing and mediating the genuine conflicts of interest that exist in any diverse society. A government that has eliminated internal disagreement has not resolved that disagreement; it has merely stopped listening to it, and the underlying tensions tend to resurface later, often violently, once suppression is no longer sustainable.

By contrast, a democracy that handles disagreement peacefully — through elections, courts, legislative negotiation, and protected protest — is doing something efficiency cannot capture: it is converting conflict into a form that does not require violence to resolve. The post-apartheid transition in South Africa is instructive here. The Truth and Reconciliation process was, by almost any efficiency standard, slow, painful, and procedurally messy. But its capacity to process an extraordinarily deep societal disagreement without descending into civil war is precisely the kind of achievement that a narrow efficiency metric would fail to register, and arguably undervalue.

I would qualify my agreement in one respect: efficiency is not irrelevant. A democracy so slow and fractured that it cannot pass a budget, respond to a public health emergency, or maintain basic infrastructure is failing its citizens in a way that matters, and citizens rightly lose faith in institutions that seem permanently gridlocked.

The statement should not be read as dismissing efficiency altogether but as correctly ranking it beneath the more fundamental capacity to manage disagreement without violence — a democracy needs enough efficiency to function, but its defining achievement, the one that distinguishes it from more efficient authoritarian alternatives, is the peaceful processing of conflict.

A government's ultimate test is not how quickly it acts but whether its citizens, disagreeing sharply and sincerely, can resolve that disagreement without turning on one another. By that standard, peaceful handling of internal conflict is a better measure of democratic health than speed of decision-making will ever be.

essays.title: A False Choice Between Building and Relieving
essays.prompt: Governments should prioritize long-term infrastructure investment over short-term economic relief, since a nation's future prosperity depends more on what it builds than on what it spends to ease immediate hardship.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which it is based. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the claim and the reason might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: The reason offered for this claim contains a comparison that does not hold up under scrutiny: that a nation's future prosperity depends "more" on infrastructure than on relief spending, as though the two operate on a single scale where more of one automatically implies less value from the other. In reality, the two serve different functions on different timescales, and treating them as competitors for priority, rather than as complementary tools to be balanced, is where both the claim and its underlying reason go wrong.

Long-term infrastructure investment is genuinely valuable, and I do not dispute the claim's underlying premise that a nation's future capacity — its transportation networks, energy grids, and digital infrastructure — shapes decades of subsequent economic activity in ways that a single relief payment cannot. Countries that under- invest in infrastructure for a generation pay a compounding cost, visible in crumbling bridges, unreliable power, and productivity losses that no amount of short-term spending elsewhere can offset after the fact.

But the claim's reasoning fails to account for a basic condition: a population in acute hardship — facing unemployment, housing insecurity, or a health crisis — cannot meaningfully benefit from investments that will not mature for a decade. Short-term relief is not merely a humanitarian nicety competing with infrastructure for the same budget line; in many cases it is a precondition for a functioning economy that can eventually support and staff the infrastructure projects the claim prioritizes. A workforce in crisis is less available, less healthy, and less able to participate in the very construction and engineering projects long-term investment requires. Prioritizing infrastructure while ignoring acute hardship can therefore undermine the human capacity needed to deliver on that infrastructure at all.

The 2008 financial crisis illustrates this interdependence well. Countries that paired infrastructure spending with direct relief to unemployed and struggling households — creating demand that kept broader economic activity from collapsing — generally recovered more robustly than those that treated relief as a lesser priority. The infrastructure investment mattered, but so did the relief spending that kept the underlying economy intact enough to make use of it.

My position, then, is not that the claim is entirely wrong about infrastructure's importance, but that its reasoning rests on a false either/or. Governments do not usually choose between building for the future and relieving present hardship as though selecting one precludes the other; the more defensible position is that responsible governance requires both, calibrated to the severity of immediate need, precisely because acute economic hardship left unaddressed can erode the very foundation — a stable, capable population — on which long-term infrastructure investment depends.

essays.title: The Case for Choice Within Obligation
essays.prompt: Some countries have adopted a policy of mandatory national service, requiring young citizens to spend one to two years in either military or civilian public service before beginning higher education or a career. What are your views on this policy?
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the policy and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: Mandatory national service asks something significant of young citizens at a formative moment in their lives, and any honest evaluation of the policy has to weigh real, well-documented benefits against a real cost: the loss of a year or two of autonomy at precisely the age when many people are first exercising it. My view is that a well-designed version of this policy, with meaningful choice built into its structure, offers more benefit than harm — but a rigid, uniformly military version does not.

The strongest case for mandatory service is social rather than purely economic: it places young people from different class, regional, and ethnic backgrounds into shared institutions and shared hardship at an age when those experiences shape lifelong attitudes. Countries with mandatory service programs often report that citizens who served alongside people unlike themselves carry more durable cross-group trust and civic engagement than those who did not, a benefit that voluntary service programs struggle to replicate because they tend to attract an already self-selected, civically-minded population rather than genuinely mixing society's full range of citizens.

The cost side of the ledger is equally real, however. A year or two is a substantial fraction of a young person's most formative period, and for students accepted into competitive academic programs or apprenticeships with narrow enrollment windows, mandatory delay is not a neutral pause but a genuine opportunity cost that can permanently alter a career trajectory. Purely military service compounds this problem for citizens whose skills, health, or convictions make military service poorly suited to them, and treating military and civilian tracks as interchangeable ignores meaningful differences in what each actually demands of a person.

This is why I distinguish between mandatory service as such and its common implementation. A policy that requires service but allows a genuine choice among substantial options — military service, but also structured civilian alternatives in healthcare, environmental restoration, education, or elder care — captures most of the social-cohesion benefit while respecting that citizens differ in aptitude and circumstance. Countries that have implemented this more flexible model, notably several in Scandinavia, report participation and civic-benefit outcomes broadly comparable to stricter systems, with substantially less resentment among those required to serve.

I therefore support mandatory national service in principle, provided it is implemented with meaningful choice of service type, reasonable accommodations for those already committed to time-sensitive academic or career paths, and a genuine investment in making civilian service tracks as substantive and respected as military ones. Without that flexibility, the policy's real social benefits risk being outweighed by resentment and the closing-off of opportunity for citizens whose circumstances the rigid version fails to accommodate.

essays.title: Responsiveness and Restraint Are Not Equally Urgent at Every Moment
essays.prompt: Some believe that laws should primarily reflect current majority public opinion, since democratic legitimacy requires responsiveness to what citizens actually want. Others believe that laws should be shaped mainly by durable constitutional principles, even when this means resisting current majority opinion. Which view more closely aligns with your own position?
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
paragraphs: Both views describe a real democratic value — responsiveness to citizens, and protection of durable principles that outlast any single majority's momentary preferences — and both can point to real historical failures of the other approach: majoritarian systems that have voted to strip minorities of basic rights, and constitutional systems whose rigidity has occasionally protected unjust arrangements against popular will that was, in fact, correct. My own position leans toward the second view, that durable constitutional principles should generally take precedence, though I think the strength of that preference depends heavily on what kind of law is at issue.

The case for majority responsiveness is strongest for laws governing policy questions where reasonable people disagree and where being wrong is correctable: tax rates, zoning regulations, agricultural subsidies. Here, binding a nation permanently to principles set by an earlier generation makes little sense; circumstances change, and a law that cannot adapt to a democratic majority's evolving judgment on these questions risks becoming an unaccountable relic that no longer serves the people it is meant to govern. Democratic legitimacy genuinely does require that this category of law remain responsive to current opinion.

The case for constitutional durability is strongest, however, for laws governing the basic rights and protections of individuals and minorities — questions where a temporary majority's preference, however sincerely held, has historically proven capable of grave and difficult-to-reverse injustice. The mid-twentieth-century American civil rights movement succeeded, in significant part, because constitutional principles of equal protection existed independently of the majority opinion of the states most resistant to desegregation; had law been required to track majority sentiment in those states at that time, the outcome would very plausibly have been different, and for the worse. This is precisely the category of decision where durable principle should resist, not follow, majority opinion.

What ultimately tips my position toward the second view, on balance, is the asymmetry of error costs. When constitutional durability wrongly resists a majority that turns out, over time, to have been correct, the harm is real but is usually eventually correctable through amendment or evolving judicial interpretation, as it has been repeatedly in many constitutional democracies. When majority responsiveness wrongly overrides a minority's basic rights, the harm is often immediate, severe, and much harder to reverse once entrenched. Given this asymmetry, I would rather a system err toward durable principle, particularly on rights-defining questions, even at some cost to responsiveness elsewhere.

My position, then, is closer to the second view but not a wholesale rejection of the first: I would restrict the primacy of majority opinion to ordinary policy questions where error is reversible, while reserving the resistance and durability of constitutional principle for the narrower, higher-stakes category of individual rights — precisely where history suggests majorities are most likely to get it wrong.

essays.title: Scarcity, Not Competence, Determines What We Value
essays.prompt: As artificial intelligence becomes capable of producing competent creative work, society will place less value on human-made art, music, and writing.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: The statement assumes that value tracks competence: that once a machine can produce technically proficient art, music, or writing, human-made versions of the same become less prized because they are no longer uniquely capable. This assumption does not match how value actually operates in creative domains, and I largely disagree with the statement, though I think it correctly identifies a real shift — just not the one it names.

Human history already contains a close analogy: the camera did not destroy the value of painting, though it made a certain kind of representational competence — accurately depicting a scene — instantly and cheaply reproducible by anyone. If value tracked competence alone, realist painting should have collapsed in prestige after the 1830s. Instead, painting redefined what it offered: expressive interpretation, a visible human hand, a specific artist's way of seeing, none of which the camera could replicate even as it outperformed painters at literal accuracy. Value migrated from raw technical competence to something competence alone had never fully captured: the meaning of the artifact as evidence of a particular human's choices, judgment, and experience.

AI-generated creative work is poised to follow the same pattern rather than the one the statement predicts. As AI systems produce technically competent music or prose with increasing ease, what becomes scarce is not competence — that becomes abundant — but the very thing competence was previously used as a proxy for: evidence that a specific human wrestled with a specific problem and made specific choices. A novel's value has never rested solely on its sentences being well-formed; readers value knowing that a particular consciousness organized those sentences in response to a particular understanding of the world. That form of value is untouched by AI's growing technical competence, because it was never primarily about technical competence to begin with.

Where the statement is right, I think, is in identifying that competence alone will stop functioning as a reliable signal of human origin, and society will likely respond by developing new signals — provenance labels, live performance, direct artist relationships, transparency about process — to identify and value work it can be confident is human-made. This is a real adjustment, but it is a shift in how value is signaled, not evidence that human-made work will be valued less.

If anything, the abundance of competent but context-less AI output may sharpen, rather than dilute, the premium placed on demonstrably human creative work, in the same way that mass-produced furniture increased rather than eliminated the market for hand-crafted pieces once buyers could reliably tell the two apart.

essays.title: Genius Has Changed Location, Not Disappeared
essays.prompt: Because scientific progress increasingly depends on large, well-funded research teams and expensive equipment, individual scientific genius is no longer the primary driver of major discoveries.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which it is based. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the claim and the reason might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: The claim's reasoning treats "large, well-funded teams" and "individual genius" as though they occupy the same causal role and therefore compete for credit — as if a discovery must be attributed to either the team's scale or an individual's insight, but not meaningfully to both. This framing is where I think the claim goes wrong: large- scale, well-resourced research has genuinely changed what discovery looks like, but it has relocated the site of individual insight rather than eliminated its importance.

It is true, and worth conceding clearly, that certain kinds of contemporary discovery are structurally impossible for an individual working alone. The detection of gravitational waves by LIGO required a global collaboration of over a thousand scientists and instruments sensitive enough to measure distortions smaller than a fraction of a proton's width — no single mind, however gifted, could have built or operated that apparatus alone. In this sense, the claim accurately describes a real structural shift in how certain major discoveries are now made.

But this shift describes changes in the scale of execution, not the disappearance of the insight that individual genius supplies. Within LIGO's thousand-person collaboration, the theoretical prediction of gravitational waves originated with Einstein's individual insight decades earlier, and even within the modern experimental effort, specific individuals — the physicists who identified how to filter noise from the interferometer's data, who recognized the significance of the September 2015 signal — supplied insights that a team's scale alone does not generate automatically. Large teams execute at a scale individuals cannot, but they do not remove the need for the kind of individual insight that determines what to look for and how to recognize it when found; they distribute that need across more specialized roles within the collaboration rather than concentrating it in one person's hands.

The clearest evidence against the claim's strong version is that well-funded teams regularly fail to produce major discoveries despite comparable resources, while a differently composed team with similar funding succeeds — a gap that resource level alone cannot explain and that is frequently attributable, in retrospective accounts by the scientists themselves, to a small number of individuals whose particular way of framing the problem proved decisive.

My position, then, is that the claim correctly identifies a real change in the scale and collaborative structure of modern science but is wrong to conclude that individual genius is no longer a primary driver. It would be more accurate to say individual insight has become a necessary but no longer sufficient condition for major discovery — still driving the crucial recognitions within a process, even as that process now requires collective scale to execute.

essays.title: Pre-Publication Verification Would Fail on Its Own Terms
essays.prompt: To reduce the spread of misinformation, social media companies should be required to verify the factual accuracy of any post before it can be published on their platforms.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the recommendation and explain how these consequences shape your position.
paragraphs: Reducing the spread of misinformation is an urgent and legitimate goal, and it is worth stating plainly that current platform moderation has failed to achieve it. But the specific recommendation — mandatory factual verification before any post can be published — would not achieve that goal either; it would instead create new, more serious problems while likely failing at the very task it is designed for. I disagree with the recommendation, primarily on grounds of feasibility and consequence rather than on the value of the underlying goal.

Consider the sheer scale involved: major platforms process hundreds of millions of posts daily, many bearing no relationship to verifiable fact at all — opinions, jokes, personal updates, creative writing. A verification requirement applied indiscriminately to this volume is not merely difficult but, with current or foreseeable technology, actually impossible to execute with the accuracy and speed users expect; either verification becomes a bottleneck that makes real-time platforms non-functional, or it is executed so hastily by automated systems that its error rate approaches, or exceeds, the misinformation problem it was meant to solve.

There is a more troubling consequence beyond feasibility. Requiring pre-publication fact-checking necessarily creates an institution empowered to decide what counts as verified truth before the public ever sees a claim, and this authority would sit with private companies operating under commercial and political pressures poorly suited to adjudicating contested, evolving, or genuinely uncertain claims — precisely the kind of claims where verification is hardest and disagreement legitimate. Early scientific findings, breaking news during a crisis, and minority political viewpoints are exactly the categories most likely to be delayed or wrongly suppressed by an imperfect verification system operating under time pressure, producing a chilling effect on legitimate speech that the recommendation's proponents do not intend but cannot avoid given the technology's real limits.

None of this means platforms should do nothing. Post-publication interventions — clear labeling of disputed claims, algorithmic de-amplification of content flagged by credible fact-checkers, transparent appeals processes, and friction added before resharing unverified claims — address the same underlying goal without requiring an impossible pre-screening of all content or creating a single point of centralized pre-publication control. These approaches have shown measurable, if partial, success in existing platform experiments, without the scale problem or chilling effect a universal verification mandate would create.

My position is therefore not that misinformation is a minor problem unworthy of serious intervention, but that this particular recommendation solves it in name only. A policy that is either technically infeasible at scale or that concentrates dangerous authority over public discourse in private hands is a poor instrument for reducing misinformation, however well-intentioned its goal.

essays.title: Convenience Removed a Skill We No Longer Notice We Need
essays.prompt: Technological convenience has made people less capable of tolerating discomfort, boredom, and delayed gratification, and this is a significant loss.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: I agree with this statement, though I think its force is easiest to see not through abstract argument but through a change in ordinary daily texture that is easy to overlook precisely because it happened gradually. A generation ago, waiting — for a letter, for a bus, for a phone call, for a photograph to be developed — was an unavoidable and frequent feature of life, and tolerating it was not a special skill but a basic condition of existing in the world. Technological convenience has not eliminated waiting from human life, but it has made avoiding it the default, and in doing so it has quietly removed the routine practice that once built a tolerance for delay and discomfort as an ordinary byproduct of daily living.

The clearest evidence is behavioral rather than anecdotal: researchers studying attention and self-regulation have documented measurable declines in sustained focus and rising discomfort with unstructured, unstimulated time, changes that track closely with the spread of smartphones and on-demand digital entertainment. This is not merely correlation dressed up as causation; the mechanism is plausible and well-understood — every moment of potential boredom now has an immediately available alternative, and skills atrophy when they are never exercised. A capacity for tolerating discomfort that is never called upon does not remain dormant and available; it degrades, the way an unused muscle weakens even though the muscle itself has not disappeared.

This loss matters beyond mere inconvenience. The capacity to tolerate discomfort and delay underlies far more consequential abilities: sustained study for a difficult exam, persistence through a failing relationship's hard conversations, patience through a career's slow early years before visible success. If convenience has eroded the foundational tolerance on which these harder, more consequential forms of endurance depend, the cost extends well beyond an inability to sit quietly in a waiting room.

I would qualify the statement in one respect: this loss is not evenly distributed or irreversible. People who deliberately practice discomfort — through meditation, demanding physical training, or simply choosing to leave devices behind for extended periods — appear able to substantially rebuild this tolerance, suggesting the underlying capacity has not vanished so much as gone unpracticed by default. The statement is right that convenience has produced a significant loss, but wrong if read as implying the loss is permanent or beyond an individual's ability to reverse through deliberate practice.

On balance, though, a loss that requires active, deliberate effort to reverse, rather than one that resolves on its own through ordinary living, is still a genuine and significant loss — and one worth naming precisely because its gradual, ambient nature makes it easy to overlook until its consequences appear in domains far more important than a moment of boredom.

essays.title: A Manufactured Trade-off
essays.prompt: Some argue that space exploration funding should be redirected toward addressing urgent problems on Earth, such as poverty and climate change. Others argue that space exploration should continue to be funded robustly, since it drives technological innovation and long-term human survival. Which view more closely aligns with your own position?
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
paragraphs: Both views in this debate share an unstated assumption worth examining before choosing between them: that space exploration funding and funding for urgent terrestrial problems draw from the same finite pool in a way that makes them genuine competitors. Once this assumption is tested against actual budget figures, the debate looks quite different, and my own position is that the first view, though well-intentioned, is built on a comparison that does not reflect the real scale of the trade-off it proposes.

The case for redirecting funds rests on a real and urgent premise: climate change and poverty cause immense, ongoing human suffering, and any dollar not spent addressing them carries a real opportunity cost. This premise is correct, and I do not dispute the underlying moral urgency. Where the view falters is in its implicit assumption that space exploration funding, if redirected, would meaningfully close the resource gap those problems represent. National space agency budgets, even at their most generous, typically represent a small fraction of a percent of national spending — NASA's annual budget, for instance, is a small fraction of comparable federal expenditure on health and social programs. Eliminating space exploration entirely would free resources nowhere near sufficient to solve poverty or climate change, both of which require multi-trillion-dollar shifts in energy infrastructure, agriculture, and global aid that dwarf space budgets by orders of magnitude.

The case for continued robust space funding, meanwhile, rests on a genuine and often underappreciated track record: technologies developed for space exploration — satellite-based climate monitoring, water purification systems, advances in materials science and solar power — have directly contributed to addressing the very terrestrial problems the first view wants to prioritize. Redirecting the relatively modest sums spent on space exploration would not simply free up equivalent resources for climate and poverty programs; it would also remove a source of innovation that has, historically, fed back into those very efforts.

My position aligns more closely with the second view, though not because space exploration is more important than addressing poverty or climate change in any absolute sense, but because the first view's proposed trade-off is largely illusory at the scale that actually exists. The genuine resource competition that matters is not between space funding and terrestrial urgency, but within the vastly larger terrestrial budget categories — defense spending, subsidies, tax policy — where redirecting comparable or greater sums would make an actual measurable difference to poverty and climate outcomes.

The debate, framed as space versus Earth, obscures where real trade-offs exist and where they do not; a more useful conversation would examine the far larger budget categories where redirected funding could genuinely move the needle on urgent problems, rather than targeting a program whose funding, even fully redirected, could not.

essays.title: The Wrong Unit of Comparison
essays.prompt: A society that emphasizes individual achievement over collective responsibility will ultimately be less successful than one that emphasizes collective responsibility over individual achievement.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: The statement asks us to compare two societies distinguished by which value they emphasize "over" the other, as though a society's success were a single scalar quantity that either orientation maximizes more efficiently. I am skeptical of this framing, because "success" is not one thing but several — innovation, social cohesion, resilience to crisis, distribution of welfare — and the two orientations the statement describes tend to trade off across these dimensions rather than one straightforwardly outperforming the other overall.

Where individual-achievement-oriented societies tend to excel is innovation and the specific kind of risk-taking that produces breakthrough advances. Environments that reward individual initiative, ownership, and personal credit tend to attract and retain people willing to pursue unconventional ideas that a more collectively-oriented culture, wary of standing apart from consensus, might discourage. The concentration of transformative technology companies in cultures that celebrate individual founders and personal wealth accumulation is not coincidental; it reflects a genuine advantage of this orientation for a specific kind of output.

Where collective-responsibility-oriented societies tend to excel is resilience and the equitable distribution of hardship, particularly during crises that individual initiative alone cannot resolve. Societies with strong collective institutions — robust social safety nets, cultural norms of mutual obligation — have historically weathered pandemics, natural disasters, and economic shocks with less severe and more evenly distributed suffering than societies where individual self-reliance is the primary cultural expectation, precisely because a collective orientation pools risk and resources in ways individual achievement alone does not.

Given this trade-off, declaring one orientation more "successful" than the other requires first specifying which outcome matters most, and reasonable people disagree about that ranking for good reasons tied to their own circumstances and values. A young, rapidly growing economy may reasonably prioritize the innovation advantages of individual achievement; an aging society facing demographic strain may reasonably prioritize the resilience advantages of collective responsibility. Neither preference is simply mistaken; each reflects a different, defensible judgment about which form of success matters more given a society's specific situation.

I therefore disagree with the statement as posed, not because collective responsibility lacks real value — it clearly matters enormously — but because the comparison assumes a single, universal measure of societal success that does not exist. The more defensible claim is not that one orientation is more successful than the other, but that each excels along different, sometimes incompatible dimensions, and the wisest societies tend to combine elements of both rather than maximizing either at the other's expense.

essays.title: Communities Set the Menu; Individuals Still Choose
essays.prompt: People are shaped more by the communities they belong to than by their own individual choices.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the claim might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: There is a strong body of evidence behind this claim, and I largely agree with it, though I would resist the strongest possible reading — that individual choice is negligible relative to community influence — in favor of a more precise formulation: communities shape the range of options and dispositions available to a person more than any individual choice does, but within that range, individual choice retains real and sometimes decisive force.

The evidence for community's outsized influence is substantial. Longitudinal studies of social mobility consistently find that neighborhood and family community are among the strongest predictors of adult outcomes — educational attainment, income, even health — outweighing measured individual traits like early academic aptitude in explaining variance across large populations. A person's early language, their baseline assumptions about what is achievable, their exposure to role models and opportunities, are set almost entirely by the community they are born into, long before they are capable of choosing anything at all. In this sense, community does not merely influence a person; it substantially constructs the person who will later be doing the choosing.

Yet this evidence supports a claim about population-level averages and probabilities, which is different from a claim about what determines any individual life. Within nearly every community, however influential, there exist individuals whose choices visibly diverge from what community influence alone would predict — a student from a community with low rates of higher education who nonetheless pursues it against considerable friction, or a person raised in a particular ideological environment who deliberately chooses a different set of values as an adult. These cases are statistically less common, which supports rather than undermines the claim's core thrust, but their existence shows individual choice is not negligible; it is the variable that explains outcomes the community-level pattern does not.

The most defensible position, then, treats community and individual choice not as competing explanations fighting for the same causal territory, but as operating at different levels: community shapes the menu of realistic options, dispositions, and default assumptions a person inherits, while individual choice determines what a person does within, and occasionally against, that menu. The claim is correct that the menu itself is set overwhelmingly by community rather than by any choice the individual made in advance — no one selects the community that shapes their earliest years.

I agree with the claim's central thrust, then, precisely because "shaped more by" allows for the individual choice that clearly still occurs; the claim would be harder to defend if it asserted that individual choice does not matter at all, but as stated, acknowledging degree rather than exclusivity, it accurately captures the outsized, foundational role community plays before individual choice ever has the chance to operate.

essays.title: Mandated Volunteering Undermines the Thing It Targets
essays.prompt: To strengthen civic life, cities should require all residents to perform a minimum number of hours of local community service each year.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the recommendation and explain how these consequences shape your position.
paragraphs: Civic life does depend on the kind of local participation that community service represents, and cities are right to be concerned about its decline. But I disagree with this specific recommendation, because it targets civic life through a mechanism — legal mandate — that is likely to erode the very quality that makes civic participation valuable in the first place: its voluntary, self-motivated character.

Research on volunteering consistently finds that the civic and psychological benefits typically associated with community service — increased trust in neighbors, a felt sense of belonging, sustained future engagement — depend heavily on the activity being chosen rather than compelled. Several studies of mandatory service programs in schools and workplaces have found that participants coerced into service report lower satisfaction and, notably, lower rates of continued voluntary engagement afterward compared to those who began volunteering by choice. Mandating an activity whose value depends substantially on its voluntariness risks converting an authentic civic behavior into a resented obligation that produces the appearance of civic engagement without its substance.

There is also a serious question of enforcement and fairness that the recommendation does not resolve. A meaningful minimum-hours requirement needs verification, which requires either an honor system vulnerable to nominal, low-effort compliance, or a bureaucratic tracking apparatus that itself consumes civic resources better spent elsewhere. Enforcement also raises equity concerns: residents working multiple jobs, caring for family members, or managing health conditions may find an hours requirement genuinely burdensome in ways that wealthier, more time-flexible residents do not, turning a policy meant to build civic solidarity into one that disproportionately penalizes residents already facing the greatest constraints on their time.

A more promising approach addresses the same underlying goal — more people meaningfully engaged in their communities — without relying on compulsion. Cities that have invested in lowering the barriers to voluntary participation, such as offering flexible micro-volunteering opportunities, matching residents' specific skills to local organizational needs, and publicly celebrating participation, have seen measurable increases in voluntary engagement without the resentment or enforcement problems a mandate creates. These interventions work with, rather than against, the voluntary character that makes civic participation valuable.

My position, then, is that the goal behind this recommendation is worth pursuing seriously, but the specific mechanism of legal compulsion is likely to be self-defeating: civic life is strengthened by genuine participation, and a policy that manufactures the appearance of participation while undermining its authentic, voluntary character is unlikely to deliver the civic renewal it intends.

essays.title: Crisis Reveals; Routine Constructs
essays.prompt: Some believe that a person's character is best judged by their actions during moments of crisis, when true priorities are revealed under pressure. Others believe that character is better judged by ordinary, everyday behavior, since anyone can rise to an exceptional occasion. Which view more closely aligns with your own position?
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
paragraphs: These two views are often treated as rivals, but I think they are answering two different, complementary questions rather than competing for the same answer: what does a crisis reveal about a person's deepest priorities, and what does routine behavior reveal about the character that person has actually built over time. My own position is that everyday behavior is the more reliable general indicator, though crisis moments carry a distinctive evidentiary value the everyday-behavior view does not fully capture.

The case for judging character by crisis behavior rests on a real psychological insight: ordinary social life offers considerable room for performance, where a person can present a curated version of themselves that everyday observers rarely have the occasion or ability to test. A crisis strips away rehearsal time and social performance pressure, forcing a decision under conditions that make sustained pretense difficult. This is genuinely revealing, and it explains why we often feel we learn something decisive about a person's character after watching how they behave when a house catches fire or a stranger needs sudden help.

The case for judging character by everyday behavior, however, addresses a limitation the crisis view does not fully answer: crises are rare, brief, and give an observer only a single data point, which is a poor basis for judging something as complex and situational as character. A person who acts admirably in one crisis might behave quite differently in another, shaped by fatigue, unrelated stress, or simple chance, while a pattern of small, consistent daily choices — how someone treats service workers, whether they follow through on minor promises, how they behave when no one is watching or keeping score — aggregates far more evidence about the values a person has actually internalized over time than any single dramatic moment can.

What ultimately favors the everyday-behavior view, in my assessment, is reliability rather than depth of insight: a crisis may reveal something true and important, but a single revealing moment is a fragile basis for a general judgment, vulnerable to circumstance in a way that a long pattern of ordinary behavior is not. Character, understood as a stable disposition rather than a momentary state, is better evidenced by consistency across many small, low-stakes moments than by performance in one high-stakes one.

I therefore lean toward the second view as the more reliable general basis for judging character, while still granting the first view's insight that crisis behavior, when it does occur, offers a uniquely hard-to-fake glimpse worth weighing alongside — though never substituting for — the broader pattern established by how a person behaves when nothing in particular is at stake.

essays.title: Judging a Guarantee by What It Removes, Not Only What It Costs
essays.prompt: Some cities have implemented policies granting all residents a guaranteed minimum income, funded through taxation, regardless of employment status. What are your views on this policy?
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the policy and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: Guaranteed minimum income programs are usually debated in terms of cost and work incentives, and these are real considerations, but I think the more decisive question is what kind of decision-making the policy removes from a person's life during their most vulnerable moments — a framing that leads me toward cautious support, with real reservations about scale and funding that any serious evaluation has to take seriously.

The strongest case for the policy is the specific kind of instability it targets. Poverty is not simply a lack of resources; it is frequently a lack of resources at exactly the moments those resources are most urgently needed — a medical emergency, a sudden job loss, a broken car that prevents a worker from reaching their job. Existing conditional assistance programs, which require applying, waiting, and proving eligibility, are poorly matched to this kind of acute, time-sensitive need; a guaranteed, unconditional income arrives regardless of circumstance and can be deployed at precisely the moment a crisis requires it, without the delay and administrative burden that conditional programs impose on people who often have the least capacity to navigate bureaucracy while in crisis.

The most serious objection — that guaranteed income removes the incentive to work — deserves genuine engagement rather than dismissal. Several controlled pilot programs, however, have found that recipients of guaranteed income largely continue working at rates similar to control groups, with modest reductions concentrated among new parents and students extending their education, outcomes that are arguably socially beneficial rather than harmful. This evidence does not settle the debate definitively, since pilot programs are smaller and shorter than a permanent citywide policy and may not fully capture long-run behavioral responses, but it substantially weakens the strongest form of the disincentive objection as commonly stated.

My genuine reservation concerns funding and scale rather than the policy's core logic. A guaranteed income funded through taxation redistributes resources, and the specific tax structure used to fund it matters enormously for whether the policy is sustainable and fair — a poorly designed funding mechanism could burden the same working- and middle-class residents the policy is meant to stabilize, undermining its own purpose.
Cities considering this policy owe residents a transparent account of exactly who bears the funding burden, not just what recipients receive.

On balance, I support piloting and carefully evaluating guaranteed minimum income policies, particularly for the acute-crisis stabilization function conditional programs handle poorly, while insisting that funding mechanisms be scrutinized with the same seriousness typically reserved for benefit design — a guarantee is only as sound as what it is guaranteed with.

essays.title: Skill Is a Means, Rarely the Measure
essays.prompt: The value of a work of art lies primarily in the skill required to produce it, rather than in the ideas or emotions it expresses.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: I disagree with this statement, and the clearest way to see why is to notice how differently we react to two works requiring comparable skill but expressing very different depth of idea. A technically virtuosic painting of a bowl of fruit and a technically virtuosic painting that reorganizes how we see grief, memory, or power are not, in ordinary aesthetic judgment, valued equally simply because both required comparable skill to produce. Skill is usually necessary for a work to succeed, but it is rarely what makes us return to a work, discuss it, or feel changed by it.

Consider how art history actually treats technical skill over time. Many of the most celebrated works in the canon — Picasso's Guernica, Munch's The Scream — are not celebrated primarily for photographic precision or technical difficulty; both artists were capable of far more conventionally skillful, realistic work and chose instead to distort form in the service of emotional and political expression. If skill alone determined value, this choice would represent a decline; instead, it is widely regarded as the moment these artists produced their most significant work, precisely because expressive power, not technical polish, drove the value judgment.

There is a genuine role for skill in this account, and I do not want to understate it: skill is usually what allows an idea or emotion to be expressed with the precision and force needed to land with an audience. A poorly executed work, however profound its underlying idea, often fails to communicate that idea effectively, and skill is frequently what closes the gap between intention and effect. In this sense, skill functions as an instrument in service of expression rather than as the source of value itself — necessary, in most cases, but not sufficient, and clearly not "primary" in the sense the statement claims.

Where the statement has some real force is in reminding us that skill is not irrelevant, and that certain movements dismissing technical craft entirely have sometimes produced work whose ideas, however interesting in a gallery placard's description, fail to move an audience without the executional force skill provides. A crude sketch expressing a profound idea is often less valuable, in practice, than the same idea rendered with genuine skill, because skill is frequently what allows the idea to be felt rather than merely stated.

My position, then, is that skill and expressive content are not independent competitors for primacy but function in a dependent relationship: skill is what allows ideas and emotions to be communicated effectively, but it is the ideas and emotions themselves, not the skill that conveys them, that constitute the primary source of a work's value.

essays.title: Monuments Convey Meaning; They Do Not Fix It
essays.prompt: Historical monuments that celebrate figures now widely regarded as morally compromised should be removed from public spaces, because public monuments necessarily endorse the figures they depict.
essays.directions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which it is based. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the claim and the reason might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
paragraphs: The reason given for this claim — that public monuments "necessarily" endorse the figures they depict — is doing most of the argumentative work here, and I think it is the reason, more than the underlying concern about morally compromised figures, that does not hold up. Monuments are not simple, fixed transmitters of a single unambiguous message; their meaning is substantially shaped by curation, context, and the ongoing conversation a society has about them, which is why removal is only one of several legitimate responses to a monument whose subject's legacy has become contested.

It is worth acknowledging directly what motivates this claim: a monument prominently placed in a public square, without context, genuinely does function close to an endorsement for most passersby, who will not stop to research the complicated historical record behind a name on a pedestal. In cases where a monument was erected specifically to celebrate an uncomplicatedly harmful legacy — Confederate monuments raised decades after the Civil War specifically to assert white supremacy during the Jim Crow era, for example — the "necessarily endorses" premise is close to accurate, because the endorsement was the monument's explicit original purpose, not merely eventually implied.

But this is not true of all cases the claim's broad language would cover. Many historical monuments depict figures whose legacies are genuinely mixed rather than uncomplicatedly harmful — founders whose accomplishments and injustices are both substantial and historically significant to understand together. For these monuments, several cities have adopted an alternative to removal: adding interpretive plaques, contextualizing exhibits, or companion installations that actively reframe the monument's meaning rather than removing the historical record altogether. This approach directly contradicts the claim's premise that a monument's meaning is fixed and unavoidable; it demonstrates that meaning can be actively renegotiated through the same public space the monument occupies, without erasing the historical presence the monument represents.

The claim's reasoning also overlooks a genuine cost to blanket removal: monuments, even to compromised figures, often serve as important physical anchors for public memory and historical reckoning. Removing a monument silently, without replacing it with any account of why, can inadvertently erase the historical conversation the removal itself was meant to provoke, leaving future generations with no visible trace of either the original valorization or the later reassessment that led to its removal.

My position is that the underlying concern — public spaces should not uncritically celebrate figures now understood to have caused serious harm — is legitimate and important, but the claim's specific reasoning, that monuments necessarily and unavoidably endorse, is too strong. Contextualization, not only removal, can address the same concern while preserving the historical record and the visible evidence of how a society's understanding of its past has changed.
